title.en: Praying through the Avos for emunah

summary.en: The Rav asks Hashem, as Magen Avraham, to protect us as He protected Avraham, the root of Klal Yisrael who passed the tests up to the Akeidah. He says the main war of Gog and Magog will be against emunah, that all prayers pass through this place, which is why Shemoneh Esrei begins with the Avos, and that here one should pray to be saved from false views and false leaders.

title.en: Tu B'Av, chassan and kallah, and accepting emunah

summary.en: The Rav notes that today is Tu B'Av, which begins the preparation for Shemini Atzeres and the joy of Hashem's union with Knesses Yisrael, like chassan and kallah, as in the last of the seven haftoros of consolation. He brings Kapitel 89 of Tehillim, which Chazal attribute to Avraham, on planting emunah in all generations, and closes by having the people accept emunah and recite the principles of faith, with the Midrash that Jews will leave galus in the merit of emunah.

catalogTitle: קבר רחל - אין עמלק נופל אלא ביד בניה של רחל

oneLiner.en: Speaking at Kever Rachel before Purim, the Rav explains that Rachel, the mother who unites Klal Yisroel, is the root of Purim and of the war against Amalek, and that the growing concealment of her grave is a sign of the final hester before the revelation.

abstract.en: After a tefilah and a short blessing, the Rav says that the light Yaakov Avinu placed in Rachel's matzeivah is still present, and recalls that the Imrei Emes davened there with Yaakov's intentions. Rachel is the akeres habayis who unites Klal Yisroel, and the thirteenth of Adar is a 'zman kehilah', a time of gathering. Following the Gemara, Purim came through Rachel's tznius in giving Leah the signs, and Amalek falls only through Rachel's children, through Moshiach ben Yosef, after which comes Moshiach ben Dovid. Her mesirus nefesh for her sister and for Binyamin, the root of Mordechai, made her the mother of Purim. Rachel still weeps over her children and Hashem still comforts her. Rachel is the revealed one, yet her grave has become covered by walls: a sign of hester within hester at the end of galus, which Purim, the megillah of hester, comes to reveal.

en: The lights and intentions that Yaakov Avinu, Yosef and the shevatim placed in Rachel's matzeivah remain there to this day.
Rachel is the akeres habayis and mother of Klal Yisroel who unites all of it, which is why her grave stands open on the road for all to reach.
Purim came about because of Rachel's tznius in handing the signs to Leah, which earned Shaul and through him Esther.
Amalek falls only by the hand of Rachel's children, through Moshiach ben Yosef, after which Moshiach ben Dovid comes.
Rachel still weeps for her children, and Hashem still comforts her that the children will return to their border.
The walls now surrounding Kever Rachel, whose grave should be revealed, are a sign of hester within hester at the end of galus, which Purim comes to reveal.

title.en: Amalek falls only by Rachel's children

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Purim came through Rachel's tznius in giving the signs, and the teaching that Amalek falls only by Rachel's children, through Moshiach ben Yosef. He explains how her mesirus nefesh for her sister and for Binyamin, the root of Mordechai, made her the mother of Purim.

title.en: Rachel weeps, Hashem comforts; revealed and hidden

summary.en: The Rav reads 'Rachel mevakah al baneha' as an ongoing weeping that Hashem still answers with 'veshavu banim ligvulam', and ties the joy of Adar to that consolation. He then contrasts Rachel, the aspect of revelation, with Leah, the aspect of concealment, in their marriages and their graves.

title.en: The covered grave: hester within hester

summary.en: The Rav compares the holiness spreading through Rachel's ohel to the halacha of an ohel, then tells of the Munkatcher Rav's fast over the building Sir Moses Montefiore put over the grave. Answering with bechirah and yediah, he sees today's walls as the lowest hester of the end of galus, which Purim, the megillah of hester, comes to reveal, and closes with a blessing for the geulah.

catalogTitle: Seeking Hashem from a Distance

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Akeidah was Avraham Avinu's hardest test because he saw Hashem only 'from a distance', confused by questions he could not answer, and that Klal Yisrael at the end of the golus is living through that same tenth test.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Parshas HaAkeidah, said every morning, and asks why the last of Avraham's ten tests was the hardest. He contrasts it with the first test, Ur Kasdim, where Avraham, searching for the truth, gave his life for a Creator he had never seen. A test, he explains from the double meaning of nisayon, is meant to raise a person, so each one is harder than the last. The Zohar points to 'he saw the place from a distance': at the Akeidah Avraham felt far from Hashem, because the command contradicted the promise that his seed would come from Yitzchak, and kashyos about Hashem's truth entered his mind. He pushed them away and went blindly. Why he did not notice that he was only told to bring Yitzchak up, as Rashi explains, is answered: when Hashem does not want a person to know, he does not know, as with Haman and the seventh of Adar. Following the Ramban that the fathers' events foreshadow the children's, the Rav says Klal Yisrael now faces the tenth test of hester panim and must hold on to emunah.

en: The Akeidah, the tenth and last of Avraham's tests, was the hardest; had he failed it, the Rav says, all the earlier tests would have been lost.
A nisayon is also a raising, like a flag (nes) held high: every test is meant to promote a person, so each test is harder than the one before.
At the Akeidah Avraham saw Hashem 'from a distance': the command to slaughter Yitzchak seemed to contradict the promise that his seed would come through Yitzchak, and kashyos made him feel estranged.
Avraham dismissed the kashyos, covered his eyes, said Shema Yisrael and went to the Akeidah blindly, without giving the questions any place in his mind.
When Hashem does not want a person to know something, even the wisest cannot figure it out; so it was with Avraham at the Akeidah and with Haman and the seventh of Adar.

Following the Ramban that the fathers' events foreshadow the children's, Klal Yisrael at the end of the golus is going through Avraham's tenth test of hester panim, and those who hold on to emunah will pass it.

title.en: The Akeidah: the hardest of the ten tests

summary.en: The Rav opens with Parshas HaAkeidah, said every morning, and asks why it is the climax of tefillah. He asks who in the room would not obey if Hashem appeared and commanded him, and notes that Avraham passed all ten tests, the Akeidah being the last and hardest.

title.en: The first test: Ur Kasdim

summary.en: The Rav tells how young Avraham searched for the truth, rejected the sun and the moon, concluded there is one Creator, defied Nimrod and was thrown into the fire unharmed. Hashem then revealed Himself to him, but in Ur Kasdim Avraham gave his life for a G-d he had never seen.

title.en: Nisayon means raising; seeing Hashem from afar

summary.en: From lashon hakodesh, where nisayon also means raising, the Rav explains that every test is meant to promote, so each is harder than the last. He then asks why the Akeidah was harder than Ur Kasdim and brings the Zohar's hint: 'he saw the Place from a distance', echoed in the haftarah of the second day of Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: Avraham's confusion and his blind faith

summary.en: The Rav describes Avraham's inner turmoil: Hashem is Emes and keeps His word, yet the command to slaughter Yitzchak contradicted the promise of seed through him. Avraham pushed the kashyos away, covered his eyes and said Shema, and went blindly; afterwards he asked the malach why Hashem had changed His mind, and was told, as Rashi brings, that he was only told to bring Yitzchak up.

title.en: When Hashem hides, one does not know

summary.en: The Rav asks how Avraham, who understood Hashem more than the malachim, missed what a child learning Rashi sees, and answers that when Hashem tests a person and does not want him to know, he does not know. He applies the same answer to Haman, who calculated that Moshe died on the seventh of Adar but did not realize he was also born then.

title.en: Maaseh avos siman labanim: the tenth test today

summary.en: The Rav calls the Akeidah a test of hester panim and brings the Ramban in Lech Lecha that the fathers' events foreshadow the children's: the famine, Pharaoh taking Sarah, the plagues and the gifts. By that pattern Klal Yisrael goes through Avraham's ten tests, and at the end of the golus faces the tenth: a whole world full of kashyos, from the Holocaust to the darkness of most of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Holding on to emunah until Mashiach

summary.en: The Rav recalls books written after the war questioning Hashem, and says that today a handful of Yidden who believe are living through Avraham's last test, with the promise that emunah will prevail. Like Avraham, one must cover one's eyes and say Shema and 'Hashem Elokeichem Emes'; the added word Emes corresponds to the 'eikev', the heels of Mashiach, which is why Avraham was told 'eikev asher shamata bekoli'.

catalogTitle: חובתו בעולמו; תפילה היא העיקר בזמן הזה; עבודה שבלב

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches bochurim that a Jew's whole life belongs to the service of Hashem, and that in our generation the main avodah is tefillah, davened with the heart and with time.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by calling the beis medrash a place of tefillah and lays the foundation from the first chapter of Mesilas Yesharim: a person must know his duty in his world. Serving Hashem is not a tax paid three times a day; eating, sleeping, earning a living and even exercise are part of the avodah when done for that purpose, as the Rambam's hired worker who sharpens his axe is paid for the whole day. He then turns to tefillah, which Chazal say people belittle. Torah is greater, yet its study is mixed with incentives, while tefillah is pure speech to Hashem; in the era before Moshiach, as the Ba'al Shem Tov taught, tefillah is the main avodah. Tefillah must be avodah of the heart: knowing the words, taking time, saying each word like counting money. He recalls how Jews once davened and announces a program of learning the meaning of davening.

en: A person must know his duty in his world: his entire life, every hour of the day, is meant for the service of Hashem.
Physical needs such as eating, sleeping and rest become part of avodas Hashem when done with that intent, and are revealed retroactively as such when the person then turns to serving Hashem.
Tefillah is a great avodah that people belittle and do not value.
Although Torah is the greater avodah, in our time, the era before Moshiach, the main avodah is tefillah.
Tefillah must be avodah of the heart: knowing what one says, turning to Hashem, and taking enough time.
The Rav announces that the beis medrash will learn the meaning of the words of davening, beginning with a few weeks on the importance of tefillah.

title.en: A place of tefillah; a person's duty in his world

summary.en: The Rav tells the bochurim that their yeshivos are places of Torah and this beis medrash a place of tefillah, and opens with the foundation from Mesilas Yesharim that a person must know his duty in his world. Avodas Hashem is not like paying taxes for set times; a Jew's whole life is devoted to it.

title.en: Eating and sleeping as part of avodah

summary.en: The Rav explains that eating, sleeping, earning a living and even exercise are for avodas Hashem, like the Rambam's worker whose axe-sharpening counts as work. If after his physical needs a person does not turn to Torah, it shows he did them for himself.

title.en: Tefillah, the belittled avodah

summary.en: The Rav says davening is a great avodah people do not recognize, and brings the Gemara that tefillah stands at the height of the world yet people belittle it. He tells how Reb Nochum of Chernobyl davened over a quarrel with a maid, since everything one needs must be asked of Hashem.

title.en: Torah is greater, yet tefillah is the main avodah now

summary.en: The Rav sets the order: Torah, then tefillah, then the other mitzvos. Yet Torah study draws many incentives, and the Toldos Yaakov Yosef writes that the Ba'al Shem Tov came mainly to strengthen tefillah; from the Arizal's time, the era before Moshiach, the main avodah is tefillah.

title.en: The sick man's diet; tefillah's purity and kavanah

summary.en: With a mashal of a sick man who cannot eat bread and meat and must live on oranges, the Rav explains why a weak generation needs tefillah. Torah lishmah is hard and mixed with motives, but tefillah is pure speech to Hashem; davening without kavanah fulfills the rabbinic obligation but not 'with all your heart'.

title.en: Avodah of the heart takes time

summary.en: The Rav explains that tefillah must come from the heart: Gemara is to be learned, davening is to be davened. It needs preparation and time; one cannot daven in twenty minutes, and he brings the Magen Avraham and the Shulchan Aruch on how long Pesukei Dezimra should take and saying words like counting money.

title.en: How Jews used to daven

summary.en: The Rav recalls an old chassid who davened word by word like counting money, contrasts today's hurried minyanim in the shtiblach with how simple Jews once davened, and describes the Satmar Rav davening slowly and aloud with the bochurim. He brings the Gemara that one who lengthens his tefillah has his days lengthened.

title.en: The chassidim harishonim and the beis medrash's aim

summary.en: The Rav tells of a tzaddik's pity for young men who never saw a Jew's avodah in davening, and brings the Gemara that the early chassidim spent nine hours a day on tefillah and their Torah was preserved. He explains the beis medrash wants to renew what was forgotten and announces learning the meaning of davening.

title.en: An old world needs tefillah

summary.en: The Rav contrasts earlier generations, when Torah alone sufficed, with today, when the world is old and bent over and the main avodah is tefillah. He tells the bochurim that their years are for Torah, yet they must give davening its proper importance, and mentions the Yesod HaAvodah of Reb Avraham of Slonim.

catalogTitle: ראשית עריסותיכם חלה תרימו לה'

oneLiner.en: The Rav tells bachurim that the signs of Moshiach are all around, and that by sanctifying the beginning of each day with zeal, guarded speech before davening, tevilah with hope for the geulah and learning Torah with reverence, they hasten their own tikkun and the redemption.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the signs Chazal give for the coming of Moshiach, comparing the present state of the world to heavy clouds with thunder and lightning before rain. There are set times when the redemption is more likely, and a final time when it must come; by every sign this period is especially ripe. Mishnayos, tefillah, tzedakah and teshuvah bring Moshiach, and since Hashem acts measure for measure, a bachur who hurries to davening and learning awakens Heaven to bring the yeshuah early. Each soul is sent down for its tikkun, and one who comes early is rectified early. The Sanzer Rav's story of the torn bekeshe shows how a garment of mitzvos riddled with excuses falls apart. The beginning must be holy: the first words of the morning, no idle talk before davening, tevilah with hope for Moshiach, and Torah learned with reverence.

en: Chazal gave signs of Moshiach so that when people see them fulfilled they know the redemption is very near, and the Rav compares the world's present turmoil to heavy clouds with thunder and lightning before rain.
Hashem runs the world measure for measure, so one who hurries to davening and learning without postponing awakens Heaven to bring the yeshuah early and not delay it.
Every soul is sent into the world to complete its tikkun, and one who comes early to davening and learning reaches his tikkun early, while one who is late delays it.

Every beginning must be sanctified, as Hashem sanctified the firstborn and the first fruits, because everything that follows is drawn after the beginning; the morning is like Rosh Hashanah of the day.
Idle talk before davening, over coffee or in the mikvah, spoils the davening, while words of chesed and chizuk to another Jew are a form of tzedakah.
Torah must be learned with reverence, aware whose Torah it is, and not casually or with levity, since the blessing over Torah says that Hashem sanctified us through it.

title.en: Clouds and thunder before the rain of geulah

summary.en: The Rav says the world is in turmoil and brings Chazal's signs of Moshiach, such as kingdoms provoking one another. He explains why the signs were given, that tzaddikim were shown propitious times for the redemption, and compares the present to heavy clouds with thunder and lightning before rain.

title.en: The final time and what brings Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav distinguishes the final time of 'be'itah', when Moshiach must come, from earlier times of 'achishenah', and says by all the signs this period is especially ripe. He lists the merits that bring Moshiach: Mishnayos and Gemara, tefillah, and tzedakah, which for a bachur means time and encouragement for a downcast friend.

title.en: Coming early: measure for measure and the soul's tikkun

summary.en: After teshuvah, the Rav explains that Hashem acts measure for measure, so hurrying to davening and learning awakens an early redemption. Each soul comes down for its tikkun, and one who comes early is rectified early; Hashem is one's shadow, and real bachurim do not live on excuses.

title.en: The Sanzer Rav and the rotten bekeshe

summary.en: The Rav tells of a man who came to the Sanzer Rav for Yom Tov in a new bekeshe of cheap rotten silk that tore at every touch, and of the Sanzer Rav's remark that this is how a person looks in the next world. He explains that the mitzvos weave the soul's garment in Gan Eden and Torah is its food, so excuses leave the garment in tatters.

title.en: Sanctifying every beginning

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem sanctified the first in many mitzvos, the firstborn and the first fruits, and called Yisroel 'reishis', because all that follows is drawn after the beginning. So the beginning of the day, week, year and zman must be holy: the first words in the morning are Modeh Ani, and the morning is the Rosh Hashanah of the day, not a time for idle chatter.

title.en: No idle talk before davening

summary.en: The Rav describes the habit of chatting over coffee and in the mikvah before davening, which the Toldos and other sefarim say spoils the davening, and urges the bachurim to try not speaking. Speech for chesed or chizuk is different; it is a form of tzedakah, and the mikvah should be brief and a real preparation for tefillah.

title.en: Tevilah in honor of Moshiach; purifying all creation

summary.en: The Rav brings that hoping for the yeshuah is a foundation of faith according to the Rambam, and recommends immersing once in the morning in honor of Moshiach's coming, as one immerses in honor of Shabbos. He explains that a tevilah below purifies the root of the soul above, and that washing negel vasser, as the Derech Hashem writes, purifies all creation, since all Jews are bound together.

title.en: Learning Torah with reverence

summary.en: The Rav says Heaven watches how bachurim learn, and that one should strive for the highest quality of learning. He decries scratching one's head or touching shoes mid-learning without washing, jokes and disrespect toward Rishonim such as Rabbeinu Tam, and learning sprawled with feet on the table, explaining from the blessing over Torah that Torah must sanctify a person. He closes that the same hour of learning and davening can be worth vastly more when done as an eved Hashem.

catalogTitle: ויחפרו בארות - של תורה ותפילה; וסתמום פלישתים - סכנת ליצנות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Yitzchak's digging of wells as the avodah of toiling in Torah and tefillah until one reaches the 'living waters', and warns that the Plishtim who stopped up the wells stand for letzanus, the mockery that cools a person's fervor in davening.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the avodah of each of the Avos and turns to Yitzchak's digging of wells. Since Hashem created everything, holiness lies in every thing; great tzaddikim could serve Hashem with all of it, while ordinary people have the mitzvos. Yitzchak's wells were deeds with meaning, and a Jew must likewise dig in the Gemara until the Torah reveals wondrous things. The Plishtim who stopped up the wells were leitzim who dismiss everything as 'just wells', and their mockery cools the desire to daven with feeling. Through the Yaaros Devash's letter, the mockery of the Chofetz Chaim and of Dovid Hamelech, the Rav shows that tefillah is the portion of a person's toil. He weighs dveikus against knowing the whole Torah, explains moments of closeness as preparation for learning, brings the levels of davening from Nishmas and the Beis Aharon, and asks the bochurim to daven with liveliness, ending with strengthening in Torah in Kislev.

en: Each of the Avos had his own avodah, and Yitzchak's was digging wells again and again.
A Jew's avodah is to dig and dig in Torah with a Gemara until he reaches the 'living waters' and the Torah reveals wondrous things; if nothing is revealed, he must dig longer and deeper.
The Plishtim who stopped up the wells were leitzim, and their mockery of learning and of long davening cools the desire for heartfelt tefillah.
The Yaaros Devash wrote that, beyond all his learning and work for the public, his portion from all his toil is the moment he stands before Hashem in tefillah, even when people laugh at him.
Moments of dveikus in tefillah, even a few times a year, do not take away from knowing the Torah; they are a preparation that makes a person's learning a different kind of Torah.
Ordinary people must daven with liveliness and excitement, at a comfortable pitch rather than shouting themselves hoarse.

title.en: The avodah of each of the Avos

summary.en: The Rav notes that each of the Avos had his own avodah: Avraham built altars, Yitzchak dug wells, Yaakov carved rods at the watering troughs. He announces that he will speak of Yitzchak's digging, and explains that because Hashem created everything, holiness lies in every part of creation.

title.en: Digging in Torah until the living waters

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's cup and table and a story of the Kotzker and the Chasam Sofer to show how great tzaddikim served Hashem with every thing, while we have the mitzvos. He explains that Yitzchak's wells were meaningful deeds, and that a Jew must dig in the Gemara until the Torah reveals wondrous things.

title.en: The Plishtim: the danger of letzanus

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Plishtim were leitzim whose jokes cool a bochur's learning and davening, citing the Midrash and the Kol Simchah: they called the wells 'just wells' and filled them with earth, the element of laziness. Yitzchak dug them again, which teaches toil in Torah and in tefillah.

title.en: The Yaaros Devash's letter on long davening

summary.en: The Rav reads a letter in the Yaaros Devash: the Rav of Königsberg asked Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz about his long Shemoneh Esrei on Rosh Hashanah, and he answered that on weekdays his learning and public duties keep him from long davening, yet he is still in Shemoneh Esrei when the tzibur says Kedushah, and people laugh at him.

title.en: Tzaddikim mocked in their time; tefillah as one's portion

summary.en: The Rav shows that tzaddikim are mocked in their lifetime, with a story of young talmidim in Radin who did not go to hear the Chofetz Chaim. He returns to the Yaaros Devash's words that tefillah is his portion from all his toil, brings the same from the Brisker Rav, and shows from Tehillim that even Dovid Hamelech was mocked and kept davening.

title.en: Dveikus and knowing the whole Torah

summary.en: The Rav calls dveikus the greatest mitzvah and brings the Shulchan Aruch HaRav that one may interrupt learning for it, except that knowing the whole Torah comes first. He explains the dispute over what that knowledge means, through the Rambam and the Beis Yosef, and concludes that ordinary people may still pause for moments of dveikus in tefillah, Nishmas or zemiros.

title.en: Tefillah as a preparation for Torah

summary.en: The Rav tells of the Gerrer Rebbe, the Imrei Emes, learning Gemara with dveikus at the Knessia Gedolah, and explains that a person who has had a moment of closeness in tefillah learns afterward with joy and a different approach. He cites the Gemara that tefillah stands at the height of the world yet people treat it lightly.

title.en: Levels of davening: Nishmas and the Beis Aharon

summary.en: The Rav brings the Vizhnitzer's reading of 'bepi yesharim' in Nishmas: the higher a person stands, the less physical motion his tefillah needs, and great tzaddikim could daven quickly with no outward sign. From the Beis Aharon he explains that tzaddikei emes are like seraphim, while others are like ofanim and chayos who rise only with a great noise.

title.en: Davening with liveliness; Kislev and Torah

summary.en: The Rav asks the bochurim to daven with warmth and excitement at a comfortable pitch, with a pleasant nusach, and tells of a bochur who answered a complaint about his loud davening by pointing to the crowd shouting at a baseball game. He closes by urging strengthening in Torah in Kislev, since the Chashmonaim had mesiras nefesh for Torah.

catalogTitle: Eisav's Final Attempt - וישקהו - And He Kissed Him

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Satan, sensing his end as Mashiach approaches, fights emunah with all his strength, and that after failing to 'bite' the Jews through persecution, Esav now 'bites with a kiss' through friendliness, assimilation and the invasion of the Jewish home.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that every person and every generation has a mitzvah of its own, and that in the generation before Mashiach that mitzvah is emunah, as Chavakuk established all the mitzvos on emunah. Because the Satan opposes whatever mitzvah is a person's success, the world today is a battlefield against emunah, just as in Mitzrayim the Jews first believed Moshe and then lost faith when the slavery grew harder. A being in mortal danger fights with new strength, like a dying candle that flares up; the Satan, who will be removed when Mashiach comes, is gasping for life. The Tosfos Yom Tov explains that it was a miracle the Kohen Gadol stayed tahor because the Satan concentrated on him alone. The Sfas Emes explains that Esav, unable to bite Yaakov, 'bit him with a kiss'. The Rav applies this to the Church's new friendliness, to assimilation, and to the Satan's 'last wish': entering the Jewish home through the internet, newspapers and television.

en: Every generation has a mitzvah of its own, and in the generation before the Geulah it is emunah.
The Satan opposes whatever mitzvah is a person's main success, so today the whole world is a battlefield against emunah.
Because the Satan will be removed when Mashiach comes, he fights now with the desperate strength of a dying being, like a candle that flares up before it goes out.
Esav, unable to destroy the Jews by persecution, now 'bites with a kiss' through friendliness and assimilation, which does more damage than the persecution did.
The Satan has been granted a 'last wish' to pass the mezuzah, and he now enters the Jewish home through the internet, newspapers and television.

title.en: Emunah, the mitzvah of our generation

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that each person and each generation has its own mitzvah, and that before Mashiach it is emunah. Since the Satan fights a person's main mitzvah, the world today is a battlefield against emunah, as in Mitzrayim, where the Jews believed Moshe and then lost faith when the slavery grew harder.

title.en: The Satan gasping for life

summary.en: The Rav explains that one in danger discovers new strength, and that the Satan, who will be removed when Mashiach comes, therefore fights emunah with all his might. He compares this to a person's last struggle and to a candle that shoots up high flames before it goes out.

title.en: The Kohen Gadol's miracle and our generation

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mishnah in Avos that the Kohen Gadol never became tamei on Yom Kippur, and the Tosfos Yom Tov's question how that is a miracle given all the precautions; the answer is that the Satan concentrated all his force on him. So too, since all signs show that this generation may see Mashiach, the Satan concentrates on it, and that is why emunah is so hard to keep today.

title.en: Vayishakehu: Esav bites with a kiss

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi and the Midrash on 'vayishakehu', that Esav wanted to bite Yaakov and kissed him instead, and the Sfas Emes's question and answer: unable to bite with a bite, he bit with a kiss. He applies it to the Church, which persecuted the Jews through the galus and now harms them far more with friendliness, assimilation and intermarriage.

title.en: The Satan's last wish: the invaded home

summary.en: The Rav points to the Pope's recent apology and visit to the Kosel as the kiss that bites, and says most Jews have fallen to it. Bringing the Gemara that the kingdom on earth resembles the kingdom of heaven, he compares the Satan to a condemned man granted a last wish: he may now pass the mezuzah and enter the Jewish home through the internet, newspapers and television. He closes that one must guard what one reads and sees and will discuss next week how to keep emunah.

catalogTitle: תפילה בידידות ובאחדות (ניגון)

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches bachurim that davening together, with love between friends, strengthens the tefillah, and that coming on time to davening and learning is no small matter, as the closed window of the mishmar of Bilgah and a story of the Chiddushei HaRim show.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with beginning davening together: Pesukei d'Zimra opens with words all say together, the Shirah at the sea was said together, and the angels praise Hashem 'together'. Like roped mountain climbers, one who slips is held by the others. Togetherness rests on love: the angels speak together because 'all are beloved'. He brings the Radbaz, who let a son daven with his friends against his mother's wish, and the friendship the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Arizal built among their disciples. Davening and learning carry each other, so a bachur cannot learn well without davening well. Turning to coming on time, he brings the window of the mishmar of Bilgah, closed by one opinion for coming late, as a closed window of heavenly blessing. A soul that came too late to the Chiddushei HaRim lost its tikkun, measure for measure. One must correct oneself before Moshiach comes.

en: Beginning davening together is a great matter: the Shirah at the sea and the praise of the angels were said together, and those who daven together hold each other up like roped climbers.
Davening together rests on love between friends; the angels say their praise together because they all love one another.
Davening well and learning well depend on each other like two feet; a bachur whose main task is learning still cannot learn well without davening well.
Coming late is no small thing: by one opinion in the Gemara the mishmar of Bilgah had its window closed for generations because it once came late.
A soul that came too late to the Chiddushei HaRim lost its tikkun, measure for measure for having come late to davening and learning in its lifetime.
One must correct oneself before Moshiach comes, because when he comes it will already be too late.

title.en: Beginning davening together

summary.en: The Rav shows from the opening of Pesukei d'Zimra in both nuschaos, from the Shirah at the sea and from the angels' praise 'together' that davening together is a great matter. He compares those davening together to mountain climbers roped to one another.

title.en: Love between friends makes the davening

summary.en: The Rav says a special angel tries to keep people from coming on time to begin together, and explains that togetherness rests on love, as with the angels who are 'all beloved' and the singers at the sea. He brings the Radbaz on davening with friends against a mother's wish, and the love the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Arizal fostered among their disciples.

title.en: Davening and learning carry each other

summary.en: The Rav explains that good davening brings good learning and the reverse, like two feet, and that only Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his companions could learn without stopping to daven. He brings the Chasam Sofer's answer about his long Shemoneh Esrei and explains why he stresses davening to yeshivah bachurim.

title.en: The closed window of Bilgah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara at the end of Sukkah about Miriam bas Bilgah and the window of the mishmar of Bilgah that was closed, and the other opinion that it was closed because the mishmar once came late. He explains the 24 windows as rooted in heavenly windows of blessing, so that coming late closes a person's flow of blessing, and adds that coming late on the first day of the Beis HaMikdash led to its destruction.

title.en: The soul that came too late

summary.en: The Rav tells, from a reliable sefer of stories of tzaddikim, how the Chiddushei HaRim, who worked to bring tikkun to souls, told one soul on his last erev Shabbos that it had come too late, and asks why the soul came late.

title.en: Measure for measure; come on time

summary.en: The Rav answers that the soul came late measure for measure, for coming late to davening and learning in its lifetime, and calls coming late the work of a great yetzer hara. Especially now, with the world in turmoil, one must correct oneself before Moshiach comes, for then it will be too late; he then leads last week's niggun.

catalogTitle: סיפורי מעשיות מהמגיד הגדול ממזריטש זצוק"ל

oneLiner.en: For the yahrzeit of the Maggid of Mezritch, the Rav tells how the Maggid repaired a dream-sin through Tehillim before coming to the Ba'al Shem Tov, and how his holy vision saved a town from a cruel poretz.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the yahrzeit of the Maggid of Mezritch, successor of the Ba'al Shem Tov and Rebbe of the great tzaddikim of his generation. He tells how the Maggid dreamt on Tisha B'Av that he made a blessing on an apple, and woke in fear of the wasted blessing. Saying Tehillim with tears, he dozed and saw a garden of trees whose fruit, leaves, branches and finally trunks fell away with each book. From this the Rav explains that every deed plants in heaven, that chiddushei Torah create new heavens which can annul a decree, as the Arizal's Shabbos zemer says. The Maggid then came to the Besht, who taught him to uproot a sin from its root. A second story shows how the Maggid delayed a messenger so that he met the official over all poritzim. The Rav closes that all Chassidus flows from the Besht through the Maggid, and urges strengthening before Moshiach.

en: Every deed a person does plants something in heaven: a mitzvah grows plantings of holiness, a sin plants for the sitra achra.
The greater the person, the greater the damage of his sins and the greater the repair of his mitzvos.
Chiddushei Torah create new heavens, and in a new heaven a decree does not yet exist, so it can be annulled.
The Ba'al Shem Tov taught the Maggid that a sin must be uprooted from its root, not only its branches.
The Maggid's holy, open eyes saw that the messenger had to be held back to meet the chief official on exactly the right day.
The Maggid's true greatness was not his wonders but spreading the Besht's avodas Hashem, so that all are his students.

candidateTopics: the Ba'al Shem Tov and his students

title.en: The Maggid's Tisha B'Av dream

summary.en: For the Maggid's yahrzeit the Rav begins the story of how he came to the Ba'al Shem Tov: he dreamt on Tisha B'Av that he made a blessing on an apple, and after weeping Tehillim he saw a garden whose fruit fell. The Rav explains that every deed plants in heaven, for holiness or for the sitra achra.

title.en: Chiddushei Torah create new heavens

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that a person's Torah chiddushim create new heavens, which can annul a decree, and shows it in the Arizal's Shabbos morning zemer: chiddushim at the Shabbos table make a new heaven with its own sun.

title.en: Five books of Tehillim and the root

summary.en: With each book of Tehillim the Maggid saw more of the garden fall, until with the fifth nothing was left. He then came to the Ba'al Shem Tov, who taught him to uproot a sin from its root.

title.en: The messenger to Petersburg

summary.en: A town suffering under a cruel poretz sends a messenger to Petersburg on the Maggid's advice; the Maggid holds him back for two days, then rushes him off, and on the way he meets the chief official over all poritzim on the Czar's birthday, who replaces the poretz.

title.en: All are students of the Maggid

summary.en: The Rav says the Maggid's greatness was spreading the Besht's avodas Hashem, from which all later Jewish holiness flows, mentions the yahrzeit of R' Baruch of Mezhibuzh, and closes with lechayim and a call to strengthen in Torah, tefillah and chesed in times of the footsteps of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: Nissan - A Time for the Renewal of Faith

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Pesach, the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu and of Yetzias Mitzrayim, is the source of emunah, and that its matzah and its springtime newness let a Jew absorb that emunah and renew himself.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the first of the Ten Commandments, which ties emunah to Yetzias Mitzrayim, and explains that Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the root of emunah. At Yetzias Mitzrayim Hashem showed that He created the world: the ten utterances of creation, which no one saw, were revealed in the ten plagues, and the last plague, of the firstborn, matches the first utterance, Bereishis. Hashem therefore wants the story told to the children and also eaten, through matzah. The Rav shows by gematria that bread holds the Divine Name three times, and matzah the Name with its filling three times. Matzah, baked fast, is above time and place, while chametz is bound to them; it is the food of emunah. Pesach and milah alone carry kareis because they bind a Jew to Avraham, his root. Nisan, the spring, is a new beginning and the month of chesed, and the Rav calls on each person to renew himself with it.

en: Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the root of emunah, and therefore it is the Yom Tov of emunah.
At Yetzias Mitzrayim Hashem revealed, through the ten plagues, the ten utterances with which He created the world.
Hashem wants Yetzias Mitzrayim not only told to the children but eaten, so that through the matzah it becomes part of a person.
Matzah is above time and place, while chametz is bound to them, so matzah is the food of emunah.
Pesach and milah are the only positive mitzvos that carry kareis, because both bind a Jew to Avraham Avinu, his root.
Nisan, the spring, is a new beginning and the month of chesed, and a person must renew himself together with all of creation.

title.en: Pesach, Avraham Avinu and the ten plagues

summary.en: The Rav shows that the first commandment ties emunah to Yetzias Mitzrayim, that Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, and that the ten plagues revealed the ten utterances of creation, with the plague of the firstborn matching Bereishis.

title.en: Telling the children and eating the story

summary.en: The Rav explains why Hashem wants Yetzias Mitzrayim passed down to every kind of child, and why He also wants it eaten: matzah baked and eaten with intent absorbs the story and makes emunah part of a person.

title.en: Lechem, matzah and the Divine Name

summary.en: The Rav explains the special standing of bread and the hidden powers Hashem placed in it, then shows by gematria that bread is three times the Name Havaya, while matzah is three times the Name with its filling, a higher bread.

title.en: Matzah above time and place

summary.en: The Rav explains that everything in this world exists in time and place, that chametz rises through time and takes up space, and that matzah, baked in haste, stays above both; it is the food of emunah, and the Haggadah is said over it so it absorbs the story.

title.en: Kareis, milah and the spring

summary.en: The Rav asks why only Pesach and milah among the positive mitzvos carry kareis, and answers that both bind a Jew to Avraham Avinu, his root. He then describes Pesach as the spring, a new beginning for the whole world.

title.en: Nisan, chesed and renewing oneself

summary.en: The Rav brings the dispute whether the world was created in Tishrei or Nisan, explains Nisan as the month of chesed, the right side, and Tishrei as din, and calls on each person to renew himself with the spring; he closes with the haftarah of the dry bones and a brachah for the Yom Tov.

catalogTitle: אגרת התניא אודות תפילה; מלוה מלכה

oneLiner.en: The Rav learns the Ba'al HaTanya's letter protesting against those who push away a long davener, tells a true story of a dybbuk driven out by the Shinava Rav, and explains why Yehuda was sent ahead to Goshen and how the Melave Malka inaugurates the new week.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a letter of the Ba'al HaTanya in Iggeres HaKodesh, written when he heard that people would not let a man who davens at length lead the prayers. Chazal say that prolonging one's tefillah prolongs life, so the Rav calls the claim of having no time a false calculation. The letter explains that in earlier generations Torah was the main avodah, but in the time before Moshiach it is tefillah, which needs contemplation of each word, and it asks for orderly, unhurried davening together. The Rav then sets out the two conditions of a proper story, a known source and a lesson, and tells, through Rabbi Elazar Brizel, how the Shinava Rav freed a girl from a dybbuk, linking it to the Chofetz Chaim's words about our test of emunah. Finally he explains that Yehuda, the root of hodaah, inaugurated Goshen, just as the Melave Malka of Dovid HaMelech inaugurates the week.

en: The Ba'al HaTanya was deeply pained to hear that a man who davens at length was kept from leading the prayers, since Chazal say that prolonging tefillah prolongs life.
In earlier generations Torah was the main avodah; in the time before Moshiach the main avodah is tefillah.
Davening means contemplating each word, which can only be done slowly, so as to awaken the hidden love in every Jew's heart before Shema.
A story worth telling needs two things: a known source, so one knows it is true, and a lesson one can take away.
The Chofetz Chaim said there would be no more dybbukim, since the test of the last generation before Moshiach is to believe without seeing.
Yehuda, named for thanking Hashem, was sent to inaugurate Goshen, and the Melave Malka, the seudah of Dovid HaMelech, likewise inaugurates the new week with songs of praise.

candidateTopics: tefillah as the avodah of ikvesa dimeshicha

title.en: The Ba'al HaTanya's letter on long davening

summary.en: The Rav introduces the Iggeres HaKodesh, letters the Ba'al HaTanya sent his chassidim, and reads one written when he heard that a man who davens at length was kept from leading the prayers. He explains the letter's argument from Chazal that prolonging tefillah prolongs life, calls the claim of 'no time' a false calculation, and explains how the chazan's repetition covers one who must leave.

title.en: Tefillah as the avodah before Moshiach

summary.en: Answering the complaint that the chassidim invented a new stringency, the letter explains that the early generations served mainly through Torah while in the time before Moshiach the main avodah is tefillah, requiring slow contemplation in Pesukei DeZimra and the blessings of Shema. The Rav adds that the early great souls could daven briefly because their minds were open and unclouded by sin, and he reads the letter's request for orderly davening together and its rules for choosing chazanim.

title.en: What makes a true story; dybbukim and emunah

summary.en: The Rav sets out two conditions for telling a story, a known source and a lesson, and presents the source of his story, Rabbi Elazar Brizel, who heard it from his father. He describes what was once seen of sinful souls fleeing the angels of destruction into a living person as a dybbuk, and brings the Chofetz Chaim's statement that there would be no more dybbukim because our generation's test is emunah amid hiddenness.

title.en: The Shinava Rav and the dybbuk

summary.en: The Rav tells how a girl possessed by a dybbuk was brought to the Shinava Rav's shalosh seudos, where the dybbuk cried out at his holy words, and after Havdalah the gabbai was sent to a certain grave and the girl was healed. He then applies it: many of us carry inner 'dybbukim', forces born of sins that keep us from learning and davening properly, which must be uprooted before Moshiach comes.

title.en: Yehuda sent to Goshen and the Melave Malka

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yaakov sent Yehuda, and not Yissachar or Levi, ahead to Goshen, and explains it through the custom of chanukas habayis: a place is inaugurated with praise of Hashem, and Yehuda is the root of hodaah and of Dovid HaMelech. So too the Melave Malka, the seudah of Dovid HaMelech, inaugurates the coming week, and he closes with blessings that the coming days of darkness in Teves turn to joy.

catalogTitle: מתינות' טהרה' לזכור את ה'' ועוד דברי הלכה והשקפה בתפילה

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches a series of practices for avodas Hashem: davening without haste, purity in the mikveh, brachos and amen, the hazmanah of leshem yichud, tefillah b'tzibbur and binding oneself to Klal Yisrael, and closes with two stories of Rabbi Moshe of Lelov.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a letter of the Ba'al HaTanya about ba'alei tefillah: one who has business and will rush should not go to the amud, weekday Shacharis should take at least an hour and a half, and on Shabbos busy people must daven at greater length. He turns to purity in the mikveh, how to conduct oneself there, and the advice to immerse with the intention of receiving the kedushah of Moshiach. He then speaks about brachos, which bring shefa to the world and are completed by amen, and about leshem yichud as hazmanah, preparation that brings kedushah to every mitzvah. He discusses starting Baruch She'amar with the tzibbur, and explains that saying a mitzvah is done in the name of all Israel protects it from any accuser. He closes with the yahrzeit of Rabbi Moshe of Lelov, his attempt to reach the Kosel and bring the geulah, and a story of a chassid saved by the Rebbe's glass.

en: Following the Ba'al HaTanya, one who will rush should not go to the amud, and weekday Shacharis should take at least an hour and a half.
In the mikveh one should guard one's eyes, go in and out quickly, and not talk, because it has its own kedushah.
A brachah draws shefa onto the whole world, and it is completed only when someone answers amen.
Leshem yichud is a hazmanah, a preparation, and preparing for a mitzvah brings kedushah to the person and to the object of the mitzvah.
One who davens at length in a fast minyan should begin Baruch She'amar with the congregation, and this counts as tefillah b'tzibbur.
Doing a mitzvah in the name of all Israel binds a person to Klal Yisrael, on whom no accuser can find a blemish.

title.en: The Ba'al HaTanya on davening without haste

summary.en: The Rav reads from a letter of the Ba'al HaTanya about ba'alei tefillah: a busy person who will rush should not go to the amud, weekday Shacharis should last at least an hour and a half, and on Shabbos those who lack time during the week must daven longer.

title.en: Purity in the mikveh and hoping for Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav speaks about the customs of going to the mikveh and how to behave there: guarding the eyes, going in and out quickly, and not talking. He then says one must hope for Moshiach every day and advises immersing with the intention of preparing to receive the kedushah of Moshiach.

title.en: Brachos, amen and leshem yichud

summary.en: The Rav explains that a brachah draws shefa onto the world, that one must remember the Ribono shel Olam when saying it, and that amen completes it. He then explains leshem yichud as a hazmanah that brings kedushah into every mitzvah, using the examples of writing tefillin and tying tzitzis.

title.en: Starting Baruch She'amar with the tzibbur

summary.en: The Rav brings that one who davens at length should begin Baruch She'amar together with the congregation, which counts as tefillah b'tzibbur. He mentions that chassidim follow the Shulchan Aruch of the Ba'al HaTanya, written at the Maggid's request, discusses where it differs from the Mishnah Berurah, and adds that saying Tehillim together after davening also belongs to the tefillah b'tzibbur.

title.en: In the name of all Israel

summary.en: The Rav explains that leshem yichud ends with the words 'in the name of all Israel', and that before davening one should accept the mitzvah of loving a fellow Jew. A mitzvah of a private person can be lost to accusers, but one done in the name of all Israel cannot be harmed, and he calls this an insurance policy for every mitzvah.

title.en: Rabbi Moshe of Lelov and the Kosel

summary.en: For the yahrzeit of Rabbi Moshe of Lelov, the Rav tells how he travelled to Eretz Yisrael to bring the geulah by reaching the Kosel, lost the Lubliner kiddush cup on the way, fell ill in Yerushalayim, was turned back by stone-throwing Arabs and passed away. He adds that one must daven for the great yeshuah for Klal Yisrael without harm to any Jew.

title.en: The chassid, the robber and the Rebbe's glass

summary.en: The Rav tells of a chassid of Rabbi Moshe of Lelov who needed a yeshuah in parnasah and received a glass from the Rebbe as a segulah for parnasah and protection. When a robber in a forest took his borrowed money, the glass became the means of his rescue and of a large reward, and the Rav closes with a blessing.

catalogTitle: דיבורים המעוררים על ענין קבלת עול מלכות שמים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that through Kerias Shema a Jew draws the acceptance of Hashem's kingship onto his own limbs and onto the whole creation, and urges the bachurim to learn before davening and to find their own shlichus where it is hardest.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the several Kerias Shemas said each day and explains that the rabbinic ones are needed for the soul: a mitzvah d'Rabbanan reaches even higher than one from the Torah, since obeying the Sages is Hashem's own command, and its leniency in doubt comes only from the Sages' own will. Kerias Shema draws kabbalas ol malchus Shamayim onto all 248 limbs, and since the world too has 248 limbs, a Jew's Shema in New York can give a Jew in Africa yiras Shamayim in his test. Rosh Hashanah is the Kerias Shema of the year, leading to the end of days, when all nations will come to Yerushalayim. With the parable of a main power switch he shows how great a Jew's every act is. He then urges learning before davening, especially on Shabbos, noting how fiercely the yetzer hara fights it, and teaches that each Jew belongs to a limb of Adam Harishon with his own shlichus, recognized by desire and by difficulty.

en: Through Kerias Shema a Jew draws kabbalas ol malchus Shamayim onto all his limbs.
A mitzvah d'Rabbanan reaches higher than a mitzvah d'Oraisa, because the Torah itself commands obeying the Sages.
Since the world also has 248 limbs, one Jew's Kerias Shema draws yiras Shamayim onto the whole creation, even onto a Jew far away.
Learning before davening is a great matter, and the yetzer hara's fierce opposition to it is itself the proof of its importance.
Every Jew belongs to a limb of Adam Harishon and has his own shlichus in the world.
A person recognizes his shlichus by two signs: a strong desire for a mitzvah, and great difficulty in doing it.

title.en: Kerias Shema and the power of a mitzvah d'Rabbanan

summary.en: The Rav lists the Kerias Shemas said each day and explains that each one draws kabbalas ol malchus Shamayim onto all the limbs. He urges saying the whole Shema before davening, especially on Shabbos, and explains why a mitzvah d'Rabbanan reaches higher than one d'Oraisa, why it is still lenient in doubt, and how Kerias Shema al hamitah destroys the harmful forces created by sins.

title.en: Kabbalas ol on the limbs of the whole world

summary.en: The Rav explains that just as a person has 248 limbs, so does the world, and a Jew who says Shema with great kavanah in New York can bring sudden yiras Shamayim to a Jew in Africa facing a test. Even washing negel vasser weakens the ruach hatumah everywhere, and a Jew's Shema reaches even the nations.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah, the end of days and Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav calls Rosh Hashanah the Kerias Shema of the year, when one asks that the kabbalas ol of the day spread over the whole world, and describes the end of days when all nations will come to Yerushalayim and the enemies of Israel will be revived for judgment. He digresses on Saddam Hussein, who saw himself as Nebuchadnezzar and used the Jewish calendar like Haman, and on Pharaoh, who knew every Divine name but Hashem's, concluding that the signs show this is the generation of Moshiach.

title.en: The main switch: how great a Jew is

summary.en: Returning to Kerias Shema, the Rav says it draws kabbalas ol onto the whole creation, even the animals and the angels, and that a Jew must know how great he is. He compares each limb to the main switch at the power company that lights all of New York: a mitzvah brings light to the highest worlds, while a sin is like a bomb. He then begins to stress learning before davening, citing Rabbi Aharon of Karlin.

title.en: Learning before davening and the yetzer hara

summary.en: The Rav admits learning before davening is hard on weekdays for those who learn late at night, but says it must be done on Shabbos. He tells how he urged the people of his beis medrash, fine and obedient Jews, to come learn before davening, yet few come; the yetzer hara lets a person eat kugel or make kiddush but blocks learning before davening, which shows how important it is.

title.en: Each Jew a limb of Adam Harishon

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Jewish souls hung on all the limbs of Adam Harishon, so each Jew comes into the world for a particular shlichus. Tzaddik or rasha is a person's own choice, but even tzaddikim differ: one from the head longs to learn, like Moshe Rabbeinu; one from the throat pours out his heart in tefillah, like Dovid Hamelech; one from the feet goes around collecting tzedakah. The stages of a life, too, correspond to the limbs.

title.en: Where it is hard, there lies the shlichus

summary.en: The Rav gives two signs of a person's shlichus: a strong desire for a mitzvah, and difficulty, since the yetzer hara fights hardest where it matters. He supports this from the Mishnah's miracle that the Kohen Gadol never became tamei on Yom Kippur, explained by the Tosafos Yom Tov, and tells the bachurim that whatever is hard for them, such as learning before davening, is their shlichus, and that now their whole task is Torah.

catalogTitle: Fortifying Emunah; השגחה פרטית

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that our emunah rests on a mesorah from Yetzias Mitzrayim and Sinai that Pesach is meant to pass down, and that complete emunah means seeing Hashem's hashgachah pratis in every detail, never saying 'if only'.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying that in the low generation before Mashiach, those raised in Torah homes carry the responsibility of passing emunah on. Our faith rests on what millions of Jews saw from Yetzias Mitzrayim to Matan Torah, written in the Torah while they were alive and handed down unchanged. Small differences between communities reflect the twelve shevatim, each with its own color, gate and path, while the Torah and Chazal's decrees bind everyone; disputes such as an eruv belong to the rabbanim, and the Chasam Sofer warns that machlokes can delay Mashiach. Pesach, the yom tov of emunah, exists to pass this down, which is why it carries kareis. Habakkuk based everything on emunah, so one must learn it, not treat it as a habit. A story of neshamos protesting endless gilgulim ends with Hashem asking only for emunah without 'would have'. The Rav illustrates hashgachah pratis and calls Pesach a time to strengthen emunah.

en: Jewish emunah rests on a mesorah no other faith has: millions saw Yetzias Mitzrayim and Matan Torah, it was written down while they were alive, and the same Sefer Torah is found wherever Jews are.
Differences in minhagim and small details between communities stem from the twelve shevatim, each with its own color, gate and path, while all of Klal Yisrael shares the Torah and Chazal's decrees.
Pesach exists to pass emunah from generation to generation, which is why it alone among the yomim tovim carries kareis.
Emunah must be learned and researched, not lived as an inherited habit, since it is the Jew's very neshamah for which whole communities gave their lives.
Complete emunah means believing that every detail is directed by Hashem, so a person never says 'would have, could have, should have'.

title.en: Our responsibility and the mesorah from Sinai

summary.en: The Rav says that in the low generation before Mashiach, those raised in Torah homes must strengthen themselves against a new, high-tech yetzer hara and pass emunah down. He describes the unparalleled mesorah: millions saw Yetzias Mitzrayim and Matan Torah, and the Sefer Torah written then is the same wherever Jews live.

title.en: Twelve shevatim, twelve colors, twelve gates

summary.en: The Rav explains that small differences in Sifrei Torah and minhagim come from the twelve shevatim, each with its own gate in heaven, stone on the choshen and flag color. He brings Rashi on the flags, a reading of 'shoftim v'shotrim' with 'lishvatecha', the gates at the end of Yechezkel, the Zohar on twelve gates for tefillah, and the twelve paths at Kriyas Yam Suf.

title.en: Machlokes, the Chasam Sofer, and what binds all

summary.en: Applying this to a dispute over an eruv, the Rav cites the Chazon Ish that each person follows his rav, and the Chasam Sofer that machlokes in the generation of great Acharonim held back Mashiach. He stresses that differences are only in small details, while the Torah and Chazal's decrees bind every Jew, and this unbroken mesorah is our strength against apikorsim.

title.en: Pesach, the yom tov of emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the mitzvah of emunah is 'Anochi Hashem Elokecha asher hotzeisicha', since the ten makkos revealed the ten maamaros of creation, and that Pesach is the yom tov for passing emunah to the children, which is why it carries kareis. Before Mashiach the yetzer hara fights hardest, so, as the Gemara says Habakkuk based all on emunah, one must learn and research emunah rather than treat it as a tradition.

title.en: The neshamos who protested their gilgulim

summary.en: After describing communities that gave their lives rather than give up emunah, the Rav tells of a tzaddik who, after Kiddush Levanah, told his talmidim what he had seen: neshamos tired of being sent down again and again went from malach to malach up to Hashem, asking what He wants of them. Hashem answers that they should go down and have emunah.

title.en: Hashgachah pratis: no 'would have'

summary.en: Hashem's condition is emunah so complete that a person never says 'would have', illustrated by a man who blames his wife for a missed train and a lost deal. The Rav describes hashgachah pratis down to a falling straw and the kernels in a loaf of bread, Hashem as the One who cares for a person more than anyone, and closes that Pesach is a time for introspection and fortifying emunah.

catalogTitle: הכנה לתפילה; חשיבות אמירת קטרת; ניסים בGulf War

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches how to prepare for davening and why saying the ketores matters so much, and sees in the missiles that harmed no one during the Gulf War open miracles, which only one who does not want to believe can deny.

abstract.en: The Rav lists ways to prepare for davening: giving tzedakah first, because a person's money is part of his nefesh and tzedakah clears away the accusers who block a mitzvah from rising; binding oneself to the tzaddikim and to the tzaddik of the generation, and accepting the mitzvah of loving one's fellow Jew; and being among the first ten in shul. He then stresses saying the ketores with the tzibbur and knowing what it means, since it drives away harmful forces, and brings the Stoliner Rebbe's assurance that it protects from illness. Turning to the Iraqi missiles that had just fallen on Eretz Yisroel without killing anyone, he calls them open miracles. Through Moshe's 'kachatzos', a story from Telz and the Sfas Emes on Pharaoh, he explains that a person who denies such wonders does not want to believe. He closes that everyone must daven and learn as Hashem's soldiers, with the ketores as their missile.

en: The Rav says one should give tzedakah before davening and before every mitzvah, since it removes the accusers who stop a mitzvah from reaching the Kisei HaKavod.

Before davening one should bind oneself to the tzaddikim and the tzaddik of the generation, and accept upon oneself the mitzvah of loving one's fellow Jew, which includes all the mitzvos as that tzaddik includes all the souls.
The Rav stresses the great value of being among the first ten in shul, with whom the Shechinah speaks in the morning.
Saying the ketores together with the tzibbur, and knowing what one is saying, counts as offering it and drives away harmful forces.
The Rav sees the missiles that fell on Eretz Yisroel without killing anyone as open miracles, which only a person who does not want to believe can deny.
Everyone must be a soldier of Hashem: learning, davening and saying the ketores are the Jews' real strength in the war.

title.en: Tzedakah before davening

summary.en: The Rav brings Chazal that one gives tzedakah before davening, explains that money is part of a person's nefesh and that tzedakah clears away the accusers who block a mitzvah, and mentions the custom of giving at Vayevarech David.

title.en: Bond with the tzaddik; the first ten

summary.en: The Rav explains binding oneself before davening to the tzaddikim, to the tzaddik of the generation and to all of Klal Yisroel through accepting 'v'ahavta l'reiacha kamocha', and then the great value of being among the first ten in shul.

title.en: Saying the ketores and knowing its meaning

summary.en: The Rav explains that the ketores stopped the plague and drives away harmful forces, that learning its parsha counts as offering it, and that this requires understanding the words, as with Torah she'b'al peh.

title.en: The Stoliner Rebbe and the Gulf War missiles

summary.en: The Rav brings the Stoliner Rebbe's words that saying ketores with a minyan protects from illness, then speaks of the Iraqi missiles fired at Eretz Yisroel in the last two days that killed no one, and calls it an open miracle that happens again and again.

title.en: Not wanting to believe: 'kachatzos' and the Telz ceiling

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara on why Moshe said 'kachatzos', explains that a person who does not want to believe will call even proven wonders a lie, and tells R' Yosef Bloch's story of the ceiling in a Telz club that stopped falling once a dead man's blood was buried.

title.en: Pharaoh's refusal and the tzaddikim's assurance

summary.en: The Rav brings the Sfas Emes that Pharaoh did not even want to want to submit, then recalls how in Hitler's time the tzaddikim davened on Har HaZeisim and assured that the enemy would not enter Eretz Yisroel, and Rommel turned back at Alexandria.

title.en: Soldiers of Hashem: a thousand for each tribe twice

summary.en: The Rav says one must still daven, brings the Midrash that 'a thousand for each tribe' is said twice because a thousand went to war and a thousand sat and learned, and concludes that learning, davening and saying the ketores are the Jews' missiles in this war.

catalogTitle: תלמוד תורה עם יראת שמים מבטלין אויבינו

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches the bachurim that Torah learning is Klal Yisroel's real weapon, as Chizkiyahu understood against Sancheiriv, so leaving the beis medrash is like deserting the army, and Adar is the time of war against Amalek, the yetzer hara.

abstract.en: The Rav opens in Adar by telling the bachurim that learning is hard, yet Klal Yisroel now needs great zechusim. He brings the Gemara that Chizkiyahu planted a sword at the beis medrash for anyone who would not learn, and notes that a person may engage in earning a living. Why then the sword? Because it was wartime with Sancheiriv, and the halacha is that a soldier who flees is cut down; Chizkiyahu knew that Israel's war is fought with Torah, and the Gemara says Sancheiriv's yoke was broken by the oil burned in the batei medrash. So the war is in the beis medrash: one must learn with strength, a niggun, warmth and love for the Torah, never with lightheadedness. Adar is a war against Amalek, which after Purim is called chametz, the yetzer hara. Amalek has a body and a soul; the soul is the yetzer hara. Those who fight well receive heavenly decorations and rise in madreigos.

en: Chizkiyahu forced learning with a sword because Torah was Israel's weapon in the war with Sancheiriv, and leaving the beis medrash was like deserting.
The Rav says the real front is in the beis medrash, and Klal Yisroel now needs great zechusim from the bachurim's learning.
Learning must be done with strength, a niggun, warmth and love of Torah, as hearing what Hashem says, never lightheadedly or lounging.
Adar, until Erev Pesach, is a time of war against Amalek, who after Purim is called chametz, both meaning the yetzer hara.
Learning, davening and guarding oneself from bad thoughts and from looking where one should not are all the war against Amalek, rewarded with heavenly decorations and higher madreigos.

title.en: The war against Sancheiriv was fought with Torah

summary.en: The Rav asks why a sword was needed and answers that it was wartime, when Sancheiriv was approaching Yerushalayim. He brings the halacha that a soldier who flees is struck down, and the Gemara that Sancheiriv's yoke was broken by the oil burned in the batei medrash, so sitting out of the beis medrash was desertion.

title.en: How to learn: with fire and love of Torah

summary.en: The Rav applies this to the present: Jews need great zechusim, so one must learn with strength, a niggun and interest, as hearing what Hashem says. He warns that learning with lightheadedness or lounging is not Torah, speaks of kissing a fallen sefer, and explains that Gemara is like burning coals, to be learned with warmth and fire.

title.en: Adar: war against Amalek and chametz

summary.en: The Rav explains that all of Adar, with its parshiyos and Purim, is a war against Amalek, who after Purim is called chametz; both are the yetzer hara in the world and in oneself, which is why chametz is treated so strictly, as the Radbaz explains. The war is fought with Torah and the mitzvos of the time, and with simcha in being a Jew.

title.en: Amalek's body and soul; heavenly decorations

summary.en: The Rav explains the two pesukim about erasing Amalek: Amalek, like a person, has a body and a soul; the body is killed physically, and the soul, the yetzer hara, is nullified. He compares those who daven and learn well to soldiers who receive decorations and promotions, which in avodas Hashem are the madreigos up to ruach hakodesh.

title.en: Sent to the front: the bachurim's war

summary.en: Like soldiers addressed before being sent to the front, the Rav tells the bachurim that Adar sends them to war against a merciless enemy, and that all of Klal Yisroel relies on their learning, davening and guarding themselves. He closes with a brachah that they be decorated, defeat Amalek and merit the world of Moshiach and the Beis HaMikdash.

catalogTitle: אהבת ישראל; עולמות של תפילהGulf War ;

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that through ahavas Yisroel a Jew joins the whole of Klal Yisroel and so completes all the mitzvos, and that the same bond carries his davening up through the worlds, leading to a call to daven in the days of mercy, also for the soldiers fighting in the Gulf War.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rashi's words that ahavas Yisroel is a great principle of the Torah, and explains through the Arizal, brought by the Bnei Yissaschar, that every Jew must fulfil all 613 mitzvos, which correspond to the limbs and give them life at techiyas hameisim. Mitzvos a person cannot do himself he completes through learning their laws and through ahavas Yisroel, which makes him a partner of every other Jew. He then turns to judging others favorably, following Rabbeinu Yonah, and shows from Dovid and Nasan that a person who judges another judges himself. Love of Hashem is measured by love of Jews, so one must share Klal Yisroel's pain. Before davening one accepts ahavas Yisroel, and davening climbs through the worlds with each kaddish as a staircase; one who comes late loses it. Tefillah is dveikus with the heart. The Rav urges davening in these days of mercy, also for the American soldiers, and tells an Apter Rav prophecy of a war that is good for the Jews.

en: Every Jew must fulfil all the mitzvos, and through ahavas Yisroel he becomes a partner in the mitzvos other Jews do, completing what he himself cannot.
Whoever judges another person is in effect judging himself, so one must judge every Jew favorably.
How much a person loves Hashem can be measured by how much he loves a Jew.
Davening rises from world to world, and each kaddish is the staircase that lifts the davener to the next world; one who comes late misses it.
Tefillah means cleaving to Hashem, and it must be with the heart and with a feeling of pleasure, not only the words.
The months from Adar to Sivan are days of mercy when the gates of tefillah are open, and they should be used to daven for Klal Yisroel and also for the soldiers fighting for the Jews.

title.en: Ahavas Yisroel completes all the mitzvos

summary.en: The Rav calls ahavas Yisroel a great principle of the Torah and brings the Arizal, via the Bnei Yissaschar, that every Jew must keep all the mitzvos, which give life to the limbs at techiyas hameisim. A mitzvah one cannot do, like pidyon haben, is completed by learning its laws and by ahavas Yisroel, which makes one a partner of the Jew who does it.

title.en: Judging favorably, and judging oneself

summary.en: The Rav lays out, following Rabbeinu Yonah, how far one must judge a tzaddik, an average person and a rasha favorably, with the Gemara's story of the worker who judged his employer favorably. He then shows from Nasan's parable to Dovid that a person who passes judgment on another is passing judgment on himself.

title.en: Love of Hashem measured by love of Jews

summary.en: The Rav shows from the order of davening that love of Hashem follows Hashem's love for Yisroel, and brings from tzaddikim that love of Hashem is measured by love of a Jew. Ahavas Yisroel means sharing the pain of Jews, including those in Eretz Yisroel in the war, and accepting ahavas Yisroel before davening opens the gates of tefillah.

title.en: The worlds of davening and the kaddish staircase

summary.en: The Rav explains that davening climbs from Asiyah to Yetzirah, Beriah and Atzilus, and that each kaddish is a staircase to the next world, with a kaddish on the way down after Shemoneh Esrei. One who comes late has missed the staircase; he can still say the words, but rising without it takes enormous kavanah.

title.en: Tefillah as dveikus, and davening for the soldiers

summary.en: The Rav defines tefillah as cleaving to Hashem, which must be felt as pleasure and done with the whole heart. He urges using the merciful months from Adar to Sivan to daven for Klal Yisroel and for the American soldiers, since there is an obligation to pray for the peace of one's country and these soldiers are fighting the wicked man of Iraq who threatens Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: Which stories of tzaddikim can be trusted

summary.en: Before telling a story of the Apter Rav, the Rav warns that most story books are false or mixed with falsehood, and that a story of tzaddikim, which is like Torah, must come from a trustworthy source. He presents the recorded stories of Reb Motel Slonimer, who accepted stories only from reliable people and whose chassid wrote them down the same day.

title.en: The Apter Rav's war that is good for the Jews

summary.en: The Rav tells, through Reb Motel Slonimer, the Apter Rav's words that before Moshiach the nations will be dragged into a war that is good for the Jews, and explains that the present war is the first such war, since the enemy wants to destroy Eretz Yisroel. He concludes that one must daven for the soldiers, describes the chapter of Tehillim said for them in his beis medrash, and urges using these days of mercy.

catalogTitle: The Disintegration of Society at the Time of עקביתא דמשיחא

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows how the signs of the generation before Mashiach listed in the Gemara in Sotah are visible today, and explains that a Jew placed in this generation is meant to withstand its tests by keeping good company and holding on to emunah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the power of a person's company: the Rambam tells one to leave a bad neighborhood, the Chazon Ish told the Satmar Rav to run to the yeshiva, and a chassid was saved from sin only by shame before his friends. The Gemara's zarzir, a bird that keeps company with the raven, belongs to its kind. Today, he says, the outside world enters a Jew's own home, and souls are sent into this generation precisely to withstand these tests, as Yosef did in Mitzrayim. He then explains why the signs of Ikvesa d'Meshicha appear on the 49th daf of Sotah, matching the 49 days of the Omer and the lowest level before redemption. Going through the Braisa, he shows its signs today: chutzpah, rising prices, a government turned to atheism, immoral universities, poverty of those from Eretz Yisrael, rebellious children and leaders who follow their congregations. Still, he concludes, one can rely on Hashem and remain a faithful Jew.

en: Company is the strongest influence on a person: what fear of Gehinnom and even a Rebbe cannot do, friends can do.
Unlike earlier generations, which lived apart from the nations, today the outside world enters the Jewish home through media and permissiveness.
Each soul is placed by Heaven into its generation for its tests and its tikkun; this generation was sent down to withstand these trials.
The signs of Ikvesa d'Meshicha appear on daf 49 of Sotah, corresponding to the 49th, lowest day of the Omer count before the giving of the Torah.
The signs of the Braisa, such as chutzpah, rising prices, a government turned to atheism and rebellion of children, are visible in today's society.
Even in the last moments before redemption, one can rely on Hashem and remain a faithful Jew.

title.en: Sotah, the Omer and the 49th level

summary.en: The Rav explains that the sotah brings a barley offering, as does the Omer on the second day of Pesach, and that the 49 days of counting lead from the highest to the lowest level before the Torah is given. Since Masechta Sotah has 49 dapim, the Braisa of Ikvesa d'Meshicha on its 49th daf speaks of the last, lowest stage before the redemption.

title.en: Chutzpah and rising prices

summary.en: The Rav applies the Braisa's first signs: chutzpah at its peak, seen in the loss of respect for teachers, in protected subversive parades and in laws that permit wrongdoing, and prices rising even where supply is plentiful.

title.en: Government turned to atheism; schools of immorality

summary.en: The Rav explains that governments were always religious, even forcing their faith on Jews, while today the state is atheist; he tells how the Ba'al Shem Tov left a wagon whose driver did not cross himself. He then reads the 'house of meeting' as the institution of higher learning, now mixed and the source of immorality.

title.en: Poverty, rebellious children and failing leaders

summary.en: The Rav describes people from Eretz Yisrael wandering abroad to collect money to marry off children, the young no longer standing for the old, children rebelling against parents, and leaders who, like a dog looking back at its master, follow their congregations. He concludes that even in these last moments one can rely on Hashem and remain a faithful Jew.

oneLiner.en: The Rav rouses bachurim to long, heartfelt davening, explaining that every word of tefillah is a heichal of Gan Eden and that every day and every person has a mission that will not come again.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Alter Rebbe's first letter in Iggeres HaKodesh: those who have time, such as melamdim and kollel yungeleit, should daven at least an hour and a half, everyone should daven longer on Shabbos, and whoever had time yet davened hastily would not be let in to hear the Rebbe's Torah. He notes that long davening is mocked, and brings the Gemara that before Mashiach the G-d-fearing will be called mad. Davening with the heart means the heart clings to every word, because, as the Chasam Sofer brings from the Ba'al Shem Tov, every word is a heichal. After a digression on how each chassid serves by his own root, he explains that stray thoughts mean being pushed out of Gan Eden. He then teaches that every day, and every person, has a unique task, as with Moshe Rabbeinu and Yosef HaTzaddik, and closes with preparing for the coming great days and for Mashiach.

en: In his letter, the Alter Rebbe asks that those who have time daven at least an hour and a half, and that everyone daven longer on Shabbos.
Davening with the heart means the heart is tied to every word, so that leaving a word is hard; understanding the words alone is davening with the head.
Every word of Torah and tefillah is a heichal, a piece of Gan Eden; stray thoughts during davening are a sign that one is being pushed out of it.
A chassid need not imitate his rebbe; each serves Hashem by the root of his soul, and what he receives from his rebbe is the point of avodah.
Every day brings its own task that will never return, and every person comes into the world for a particular moment of trial.
Great days are coming, and one must prepare a garment for greeting Mashiach, woven of Torah, mitzvos and tefillah.
